newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Consumers to cushion slowdown in British economy.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Consumers to cushion slowdown in British economy.

text.p: A tight government grip on the public purse combined with strong currency problems faced by producers will slow the galloping British economy to a canter over the next two years, a Reuters survey showed on Monday.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is set to peak at 3.7 percent in the third quarter of this year thanks to continued strong consumer demand, an average of the forecasts showed.

Reuters surveyed 29 economists between July 7 and 9 in its quarterly survey of the British economy and found them to be in broad agreement with Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's GDP targets set in his July 2 budget.
He said he was aiming for 3.25 percent growth in 1997, just less than the average survey prediction of 3.4 percent. The mean for 1998 was in line with Brown's target of 2.5 percent.

"We've got very strong consumer spending growth and that's pushing the economy up quite substantially," said David Bloom, UK economist at HSBC James Capel, who predicted growth of 5.3 percent in the final quarter of this year -- the highest forecast in the survey.
Bloom said windfall gains, rising house prices, higher average earnings, falling unemployment and the effect of a strong stock market would leave the consumer feeling optimistic.

Growth is expected to ease after next year, with the average prediction from 15 economists putting GDP at 1.8 percent in Q1 1999, as the 5.5 billion sterling fiscal tightening announced in the budget takes its toll on consumers, and manufacturers are hit by the ever-stronger pound.
Sterling has soared by 30 percent against the mark since last July and jumped last week to six-month highs against the dollar.
"These factors will have knock-on effects on employment and consumer confidence," said Trevor Williams, senior economist at Lloyds TSB Group.

In a further blow to manufacturers, the Bank of England's monetary policy committee raised base rates by 25 basis points to 6.75 percent last Thursday, a move which is expected to increase the demand for sterling and push the currency still higher.
"The strong exchange rate not only reduces their export potential but it also increases competition from imports," Williams said.

Williams was one of the most downbeat in the survey about prospects for manufacturing, predicting a drop in industrial production growth to just 0.7 percent in the second quarter of 1998 before a foray into negative territory.

Figures for May 1997 showed industrial production down 0.2 percent year-on-year, and while the underlying trend for production remained weak, most economists did not expect to see a repeat of such a large drop.
The average of 16 forecasts put production growth at 1.6 percent in 1997 and 1.8 percent in 1998.
Some economists thought the cash-rich consumer may yet come to the rescue of British manufacturers.
"Obviously the external sector and exports will be quite weak, but the producer could get an upside surprise from the strength of the domestic economy," said HSBC's Bloom.
